extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, rejecting, and overcoming double patenting issues during U.S. patent examination, including statutory and non-statutory (obviousness-type and anticipation) double patenting and use of terminal disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double Patenting Prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant (or assignee) is prohibited from obtaining two patents for the same invention, and also prohibited from obtaining a patent for an invention that is an obvious variation of an invention for which the applicant (or assignee) already has a patent (unless certain conditions are met).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: Prevents unjustified extension of exclusive rights so that after expiration the public may freely use the claimed invention and obvious modifications thereof. This is grounded in the constitutional goal to 'promote the progress of science and useful arts' by granting a limited exclusive right in exchange for disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Double Patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Two general types: Statutory Double Patenting and Non-Statutory Obviousness-Type Double Patenting (which includes rejections based on obviousness analysis and rejections based on anticipation analysis). Also non-statutory rejections based solely on improper timewise extension of patent rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish which type applies because available remedies differ (e.g., terminal disclaimer can overcome ODP but not statutory double patenting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Double Patenting (35 U.S.C. 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory double patenting asks whether the 'same invention' is being claimed twice — i.e., identical subject matter being claimed in two patents/applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliable test: Is there an embodiment that falls within the scope of one claim but not the other? Could one claim be literally infringed without literally infringing the other claim? Remedies: Amend or cancel claims. A terminal disclaimer is NOT sufficient to overcome a statutory double patenting rejection. Declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 are NOT sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Statutory Obviousness-Type Double Patenting (ODP-Obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejection based on an obviousness analysis that the claimed invention would have been an obvious variation of an invention defined in a claim in a patent (or copending application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any obviousness-type double patenting rejection should make clear: (1) the differences between the examined claim and the claim in the reference patent or copending application, and (2) the reasons for concluding that the claim at issue would have been an obvious variation. Reliance on the specification of a potentially conflicting patent or application is generally prohibited (limited exceptions apply). Declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 are NOT sufficient to overcome such a rejection. Remedies include amending/canceling claims, filing argument/documentary evidence, or filing a proper terminal disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Statutory ODP — Anticipation-Based Rejection (ODP-Anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Situation where an examined claim is generic to (fully encompasses) a claim in the potentially conflicting patent or application and is therefore anticipated by that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written rejection: No Graham v. Deere (obviousness) analysis is needed; the rejection must explain how the examined claim is anticipated. Caution: A generic claim does not usually anticipate a species/subgenus claim; domination or overlapping generic claims do not usually anticipate one another. If ODP-Anticipation does not apply, an ODP-Obviousness analysis may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Rejection Content Requirements for ODP-Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Any obviousness-type double patenting rejection based on an obviousness analysis should make clear the differences between the examined claim and the reference claim and the reasons for concluding the examined claim would have been an obvious variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must articulate both the claim differences and the rationale supporting an obviousness conclusion (i.e., factual findings and reasoning). This distinguishes an ODP-Obviousness rejection from a mere conclusory assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences Between 35 U.S.C. 103 Analysis and ODP-Obviousness Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness) analysis uses prior art within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 102; ODP-Obviousness analysis uses claims of a potentially conflicting patent or application (alone or with 102 prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance on the specification of a potentially conflicting patent/application is generally prohibited in ODP analyses, except for limited uses (e.g., dictionary or claim-support). Understand which source constitutes the 'reference' for the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper Uses of Disclosure of a Potentially Conflicting Patent/Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions to the general prohibition on using the disclosure of a potentially conflicting patent/application include: (1) using it as a dictionary for claim terminology, and (2) portions of the disclosure that provide support for the claims in the potentially conflicting patent/application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should avoid treating the specification of a conflicting patent as prior art except for these limited purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on Claims for Double Patenting Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the claims of the potentially conflicting patent/application to the examined claims; the use of the specification of the potentially conflicting patent/application is generally prohibited (with limited exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis is primarily claim-to-claim; assess literal scope overlap, generic/species relationships, and whether one claim could be literally infringed without infringing the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: ODP-Anticipation — Caution Regarding Generic and Species Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic claim does not usually anticipate a species; overlapping generic claims do not usually anticipate one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer anticipation simply from broad-to-narrow claim overlap (domination). Where anticipation is not established, consider ODP-Obviousness instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domination
rubrics_metrics.description: Domination: Broad or generic claims in one patent fully encompass narrower claims in another patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domination by itself cannot support a double patenting rejection, but domination does not preclude a double patenting rejection. Examiners must analyze whether the domination actually establishes statutory or non-statutory double patenting per the applicable tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Rule — One-Way vs. Two-Way Test
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the One-Way Test unless all three of the following apply: (1) the examined application has an effective U.S. filing date before that of a potentially conflicting patent; (2) there is sufficient evidence of record that the claims could not have been filed in the same application; and (3) there is sufficient evidence of record that there was administrative delay on the part of the Office in the application being examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when all three conditions are met should a Two-Way test be applied; otherwise, use the One-Way approach for double patenting timing comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double Patenting vs. Art (Prior Art) Rejection Distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Double patenting compares claims (with limited use of the disclosure of the potentially conflicting patent/application) and can be overcome by a terminal disclaimer (ODP only). An art rejection uses the reference for all it fairly teaches and cannot be overcome by a terminal disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate an art rejection with a double patenting rejection; the legal bases, evidentiary sources, and remedies differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to Disclose (MPEP 2001.06)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants have a duty to disclose to the USPTO all material information they are aware of regardless of the source or how they become aware of the information; the duty extends to information known prior to or at filing or learned during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must bring to the examiner's attention copending U.S. applications which are 'material to patentability' of the application in question (see Dayco Products Inc. v. Total Containment Inc., 66 USPQ2d 1801). Failure to disclose material copending applications can violate the duty of candor and good faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 121 Protection (Third Sentence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third sentence of 35 U.S.C. 121: a patent issuing on an application subject to a restriction requirement, or on an application filed as a result of such a requirement, shall not be used as a reference against a divisional application or the original application or any patent issued on either of them, if the divisional application is filed before the issuance of the patent on the other application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory protection shields divisional/original applications from being used as references in certain restriction/divisional situations; examiners must check the procedural facts (restriction requirement timing, filing dates, issuance dates) before relying on a patent as a reference under 121.

rubrics_metrics.name: When 35 U.S.C. 121 Does Not Apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations where the 121 prohibition does not apply include: (1) two or more applications filed with no restriction requirement made; (2) claims amended such that they are not commensurate with the restriction requirement (see Geneva Pharmaceuticals Inc. v. GlaxoSmithKline PLC); (3) lack of unity made in a PCT application (no restriction in US application); (4) examiner withdraws restriction before patent issues (linking claim practice followed and generic claim allowed); and (5) claims are directed to identical subject matter (statutory double patenting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the procedural history (restriction requirements, amendments, PCT unity findings, examiner actions) before applying 121 protection; if 121 does not apply, other double patenting analyses may be available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal Disclaimer — Purpose and Basic Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer is a legal document that ensures the term for a patent granted on the examined application will not extend past the expiration of the term of the conflicting patent or a patent granted on a conflicting application, and it requires common ownership between the examined application and the conflicting patent/patent granted on the conflicting application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a proper terminal disclaimer can remove the potential harm to the public caused by timewise extension of patent rights and is an available remedy for non-statutory double patenting (ODP) but not for statutory double patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal Disclaimer — Operative Details and Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer 'must operate with respect to all claims in the patent,' is 'not an admission of the propriety of the rejection,' and is 'effective only with respect to the application identified in the disclaimer, unless by its terms it extends to continuing applications.' A fee is required for each terminal disclaimer filed. A terminal disclaimer is required even in applications filed on or after June 8, 1995.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when patents would expire on the same day, a terminal disclaimer is required to ensure enforceability only as long as they are commonly owned; ensure correct identification of application numbers and payment of fees. Terminal disclaimer effectiveness is limited to the application(s) identified unless it explicitly extends.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Overcome a Proper Statutory Double Patenting Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory double patenting can be overcome by amending the claims or canceling the claims. A terminal disclaimer is NOT sufficient, and declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 are NOT sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because statutory DP is a same-invention/identical-subject-matter problem, only substantive change to the claim set (or cancellation) resolves it.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to Overcome a Proper Non-Statutory Double Patenting Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-statutory double patenting rejections (all types) may be overcome by amending the claims, canceling the claims, filing argument and/or documentary evidence, or filing a proper terminal disclaimer. Declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 are NOT sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimers are an accepted procedural remedy for ODP but do not address statutory double patenting. When relying on arguments or evidence, ensure the examiner's written rejection criteria (differences and reasons) are addressed.
